title: Morning Brief, Thursday 12 Nov 2026
notes:
Morning Brief, Thursday 12 November 2026

AI

1. Google opens up Gemini 4 Carbon, its deepest-thinking model
Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-carbon-now-available/
Google's strongest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, has gone from a small circle of cyber-defence teams to every paying developer and top-tier subscriber. Think of it as the patient sibling: where the everyday model answers quickly, Carbon spends more effort exploring, double-checking and running its own verification loops before it commits. Google pairs it with a preview of "swarm" mode in its Antigravity coding tool, where one prompt spins up a team of agents that split the work and review each other. The striking claims are on security, with partners saying it found fresh zero-day holes in big software services in an afternoon. Caveat: the benchmark wins are Google's own reporting, and the low launch price doubles after November.

2. Anthropic ships one brain under two names: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
Source: https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2
Anthropic released a new top model in two versions that are literally the same underlying system. Fable is the public face, wrapped in safety filters that block risky cyber-attack and biology requests; Mythos is the unfiltered twin, available only to vetted security and life-science teams. It is a neat answer to the "dual-use" dilemma: share the brainpower widely, keep the dangerous skills behind a door. The showcase stories are wild, from a team of about a thousand agents formalising the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in about a day, to designing three working gadgets from scratch. Caveat: Anthropic amended the Fermat description to clarify how much help the agents were given.

3. AI-assisted hunting finds memory-safety bugs inside Rust itself
Source: https://forge-blog.github.io/posts/rust-std-memory-safety/
Rust is famous for promising that "safe" code can't corrupt memory. Microsoft's FORGE Lab, using an AI vulnerability scanner as a research partner, found several places in Rust's own standard library where that promise quietly broke. The bugs fall into three kinds of misplaced trust: assuming code never crashes halfway through, assuming user-supplied pieces behave honestly, and assuming the operating system's shared state stays put. One bug had been hiding for nearly eleven years. The interesting twist is that AI agents seem good at the third kind, because they understand how the surrounding system behaves. Caveat: each bug needs an unusual setup, so it isn't an automatic hole in Rust programs, and two reports are still open.

4. Gemini Robotics 2.5 puts a humanoid to work on a Mercedes production line
Source: https://deepmind.google/blog/gemini-robotics-2-5-accelerates-real-world-physical-intelligence/
Google DeepMind's new robot brain sees, understands instructions and moves hands, and it learns new skills faster than before, from tying a bow on a gift to pipetting liquid. The headline test was real: Apptronik's Apollo humanoid sorted metal car brackets from bulk bins into trays at Mercedes-Benz factories, succeeding almost every time. Part of the speed-up came from using the big Gemini model as a kind of imagination engine, generating thousands of simulated practice runs from a single camera view. DeepMind also released an open test for "jailbreaking" robots with disguised unsafe requests. Caveat: it's going to partners only, and the factory work was a proof of concept.

CRYPTO & TRADING

5. Solana's Agave client speeds up its upgrade cycle and plans big rent cuts
Source: https://solanacompass.com/news/anzas-agave-v45-schedule-cuts-solana-mainnet-adoption-to-two-steps-and-pauses-feature-activations-for-breakpoint
Anza, the team behind Solana's main validator software, is shortening how new versions roll out: instead of three cautious steps, version 4.5 goes to a volunteer fifth of the network first, then to everyone a week later, around early December. Release work pauses for the Breakpoint conference. Two changes users will feel: "rent", the refundable deposit every account must hold, keeps shrinking toward a ninety percent cut, making new accounts cheaper; and "direct mapping" lets programs work on account data in place instead of copying it back and forth, which should make apps faster. Caveat: dates are targets and can slip.

6. Crypto bounces after the inflation scare, helped by Deutsche Bank custody going live
Source: https://www.cryptotimes.io/2026/11/11/crypto-market-up-bitcoin-price-reclaims-74k-as-eth-xrp-sol-rally-on-deutsche-bank-custody-launch/
After a hot US inflation report knocked prices down and wiped out lots of leveraged bets, crypto clawed back on Wednesday, with Bitcoin back around seventy-four thousand dollars and Solana leading the rebound. The fundamental nudge came from Deutsche Bank, whose crypto custody service is now live for institutional clients in Europe, one more regulated door into Bitcoin and Ether. Part of the bounce was short sellers being forced to buy back. The opportunity: momentum is turning and big institutions keep building rails. The risk: spot Bitcoin funds have seen several straight days of outflows, and the last rally stalled around eighty-one thousand. Not financial advice.

7. Binance lets users buy tokenized stocks straight from local currency
Source: https://www.binance.com/en/support/announcement/99ee5d4197904f45a5337987ea72c22b
Binance now lets eligible users buy its "bStocks", blockchain tokens each backed by a real share held at a custodian, directly with dozens of local currencies, by card or phone wallet, and sell back to cash without touching crypto in between. It's part of a bigger trend of stocks moving onto crypto rails, alongside Chainlink's Asian equity price feeds. It also signals Binance pushing products again after its huge October hack recovery. The fine print matters: these are certificates issued by a Binance affiliate under Abu Dhabi rules, not direct share ownership, and availability depends on where you live. Not financial advice.

SCIENCE

8. A brand-new way of looking confirms the M87 black hole's ring of light
Source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11241-9
The famous first picture of a black hole showed a glowing ring around a dark centre, but because the image was stitched together from sparse radio data, some critics argued the ring might be an artefact of the processing. A team in Australia has now rebuilt the picture with a completely independent method that doesn't assume any shape in advance and relies only on measurements immune to telescope calibration errors. The ring came back, clear as before, matching a black hole of roughly six and a half billion suns. It's science doing what it should: checking a landmark result from scratch and finding it holds.

9. Two monster black holes, side by side, at cosmic dawn
Source: https://phys.org/news/2026-11-earliest-compact-quasar-pair-poses.html
Using the Webb telescope and the Gemini North telescope in Hawai'i, astronomers found the oldest close pair of quasars ever seen, two feeding supermassive black holes shining when the universe was under a billion years old. Nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, they are already as heavy as giants we see nearby today, and they sit closer together than the width of our galaxy. That is a puzzle: nobody can fully explain how even one black hole grew that big so fast, let alone two. The team suspects they live in an unusually dense knot of the early universe where colliding galaxies fed them. Paper: The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

10. An invisible, overweight neutron star tugging on a red giant
Source: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/newfound-invisible-object-in-space-could-be-a-rare-supermassive-neutron-star/
In Pisces, a red giant star is wobbling back and forth as though something heavy is circling it, yet that something gives off no light. After ruling out other options, Chinese astronomers argue it is most likely a neutron star, the city-sized crushed core of an exploded star, but an unusually heavy one, well above the typical weight. The mystery is where the extra mass came from: normally a neutron star bulks up by stealing gas from its neighbour, but this orbit looks too wide for that. Heavy neutron stars are prized because they test the extreme physics of matter inside them. Published in Science Advances; the identification is still an inference.
